questions.question: Adjustments exist because:
options: The ledger describes the year as recorded, and some year-end truths have no document yet
The trial balance never balances at year end
GAAP forbids monthly recording
The owner wants a higher profit

questions.question: The post-adjustment trial balance is:
options: The ledger as the year's routine left it
The version drawn after the adjustments — the one the final accounts are built from
A list of adjustments only
Another name for the income statement

questions.question: The principle that powers every adjustment is:
options: Historical cost
Going concern
Matching — this year's statement carries this year's incomes and expenses, no more, no less
Double entry

questions.question: Prudence demands that losses be recognised:
options: When the owner approves them
At the start of the next year
Only if material
The moment they are discovered — never when convenient

questions.question: Stationery shows R1 500 and the cupboard holds R300 unused. The adjustment is:
options: Credit Stationery R300; debit Consumable Stores on Hand R300 — the expense reports the R1 200 consumed
Debit Stationery R300; credit Bank R300
Credit Stationery R1 200; debit Consumable Stores on Hand R1 200
No entry — stationery is always fully expensed

questions.question: The Trading Stock account claims R3 100; the stocktake counts R2 880. The books must:
options: Adjust the count upward to R3 100
Wait a month for the stock to reappear
Credit Trading Stock R220 and debit Trading Stock Deficit R220 — the count is the fact
Debit Trading Stock R220

questions.question: The Trading Stock Deficit account is:
options: An asset carried to next year
An expense recognising the loss now, as prudence demands
A liability owed to the supplier
Part of Cost of Sales

questions.question: After the adjustments, the trial balance still levels because:
options: Adjustments are recorded outside the ledger
The difference is posted to Capital
Only debits were adjusted
Every adjustment was itself a complete double entry

subtopics.title: The Final Accounts — Trading, and Profit and Loss

questions.question: The Trading account's credit balance of R50 000 (Sales R150 000 less Cost of Sales R100 000) is:
options: The gross profit — the trading result before any running cost
The net profit
The owner's drawings
The mark-up percentage

questions.question: The gross profit confirms the pricing policy because:
options: Gross profit always equals half of sales
Fifty percent on a cost of R100 000 is exactly R50 000
Sales equal cost of sales
The mark-up is irrelevant to gross profit

questions.question: Profit and Loss assembles R59 000 of earnings (gross profit plus rent income) and drains R21 400 of expenses, leaving:
options: R37 600 net profit

questions.question: The net profit's final transfer is:
options: Debit Capital; credit Bank
Debit Trading; credit Profit and Loss
It stays in Profit and Loss for next year
Debit Profit and Loss; credit Capital — the profit belongs to the owner

questions.question: The correct order of the year-end run is:
options: Pre-adjustment trial balance; adjustments; post-adjustment trial balance; final accounts; profit to Capital; statements
Final accounts; adjustments; trial balance; statements
Statements; final accounts; adjustments
Adjustments; final accounts; pre-adjustment trial balance

questions.question: Preparing final accounts BEFORE adjusting produces:
options: A faster year end with no drawbacks
A profit wrong by every unadjusted rand
The same result in a different order
A balanced but empty ledger

questions.question: The stationery adjustment appears downstream as:
options: Only a change to the expense
Only a new asset
A changed expense in Profit and Loss AND an asset among the year-end balances — one fact, two appearances
A change to Sales

questions.question: The classic lost mark in this topic is:
options: Using a pencil for the trial balance
Closing Sales before Cost of Sales
Naming GAAP principles unnecessarily
The half-adjustment — naming only one account of the double entry

questions.question: The diary cannot simply be photocopied into a report card because:
options: Some of its lines have drifted from the truth — unused stationery, uncounted stock
Diaries are written in pencil
Report cards use different currency
The owner has not read the diary

questions.question: 'The diary isn't lying; it just doesn't know what it hasn't been told' refers to:
options: Fraud in the bookkeeping
Recording that follows documents, while some year-end truths have no document yet
The bookkeeper's poor memory
Errors in the journals

questions.question: Year-end's two jobs, in order, are:
options: Squeeze first, tidy second
Count the cash, then close the shop
Tidy the diary to match the real shop, then squeeze it into the report card
Draw the statements, then adjust them

subtopics.title: Tidying the Room Before the Photo

questions.question: The R300 of untouched paper and ink becomes:
options: This year's expense
A donation
Part of Trading Stock
A small asset — a parcel handed across the year-end line to next year

questions.question: 'The shelf wins — always' means:
options: The physical count is the fact, and the books must come down to match it
Stock on shelves is never stolen
The books outrank the stocktake
Shelf stock is valued at selling price

questions.question: 'Bad news goes on the card immediately; good news waits to be proven' is:
options: The matching principle
The prudence principle — the reason report cards can be trusted
The going concern principle
The historical cost principle

questions.question: After both tidyings, the next move is:
options: Straight to the financial statements
Re-counting the stock
A re-check that the tidied diary still balances — the post-adjustment trial balance
Transferring profit to Capital

subtopics.title: Two Sieves and the Owner's Jar

questions.question: Sieve one catches:
options: Every cost of running the shop
The rent income
The owner's drawings
Only the buying-and-selling story — sales in, cost of those goods in, gross profit stays

questions.question: Sieve two assembles R59 000 and drains R21 400, leaving:
options: R37 600 — the net profit, what the year truly earned
R50 000 — the gross profit

questions.question: The net profit lands in the owner's jar because:
options: The bank requires it
The profit was always the owner's — the shop was working it up all year, so it transfers to Capital
Profit must be spent within the year
The jar earns interest

questions.question: After the transfers, the nominal accounts stand:
options: At their year-end balances
Overdrawn
Empty — swept clean, ready for the new year
Frozen until the audit
